1.e4 d5 2.exd5.strategy: Takes the pawn and makes Black decide how to win it back. Recapturing at once with the queen costs time, because White can develop with gain of tempo against it; delaying with a knight keeps Black's pieces active but lets White build in the centre. It is the move that gives White real chances of an advantage, which is why it is played almost every time.

1.e4 d5 2.Nc3.name: Dunst Opening
1.e4 d5 2.Nc3.background: Named after Ted A. Dunst (1907–1985), a New York master who analysed and played 1.Nc3, which gave the opening its most popular name in the United States. The same position arises from 1.Nc3 d5 2.e4; Blackburne played 1.Nc3 against Josef Noa in the London 1883 tournament.
1.e4 d5 2.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and avoids the main lines, but gives up the initiative that taking on d5 offers. Black can gain space by pushing the d-pawn and cramping the knight, or trade on e4 and develop easily, so Black gets a comfortable game.

1.e4 d5 2.d4.name: Blackmar–Diemer Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.d4.background: Grew out of the Blackmar Gambit, named after Armand Blackmar, a New Orleans player of the late nineteenth century who published the first analysis of 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.f3. Ignatz von Popiel introduced 3.Nc3 in 1889, and the German master Emil Josef Diemer (1908–1990) popularised the modern 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3. It can also be reached from the Scandinavian Defence with 2.d4.
1.e4 d5 2.d4.strategy: Offers the e4-pawn for a strong centre, quick development and open lines, a gambit that is rarely seen at top level because Black has several sound ways to meet it. Black can also decline the pawn and transpose into familiar set-ups.

1.e4 d5 2.Nf3.name: Tennison Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.Nf3.background: Named after Otto Mandrup Tennison (1834–1909), a Danish-born amateur who moved to the United States in 1854, played in the New Orleans chess clubs and was the first to research the opening significantly. It is also known as the Lemberg, Lviv or Polish Gambit, and 1.Nf3 d5 2.e4 reaches the same position.
1.e4 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: Sacrifices the e4-pawn for quick piece play: after 2.Nf3 dxe4 3.Ng5 White hopes to win it back or to hit f7. Black keeps the pawn or returns it at the right moment, and stands better either way.

1.e4 d5 2.e5.strategy: Gains space but releases the central tension and poses Black no problems. Black develops the c8-bishop outside the pawn chain and then builds a favourable French-like structure in which the e5-pawn needs constant support.

1.e4 d5 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 and opens the d1–a4 diagonal, but leaves e4 attacked. After 2.c3 dxe4 3.Qa4+ c6 4.Qxe4 the pawn is back, but Black develops with tempo against the queen.

1.e4 d5 2.c4.strategy: Hits d5 a second time, but gives up the e4-pawn: after 2.c4 dxe4 the c4-pawn blocks the fourth rank, so Qa4+ does not win e4 back, and White plays a pawn down. Black can also gain space by pushing the d-pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.d3.strategy: Defends e4 solidly but shuts in the diagonal of the f1-bishop. After 2.d3 dxe4 3.dxe4 Qxd1+ 4.Kxd1 White loses the right to castle for a harmless queenless position, and Black develops without difficulty.

1.e4 d5 2.f3.strategy: Supports e4, but takes f3 from the king's knight and opens the e1–h4 diagonal to the king. After 2.f3 dxe4 3.fxe4 e5 the open diagonal already allows …Qh4+, and White has weakened the king for nothing.

1.e4 d5 2.Qe2.strategy: Defends e4 with the queen, which blocks the f1-bishop. After 2.Qe2 dxe4 3.Qxe4 Nf6 the queen is hit at once and must lose another tempo, so Black develops with gain of time.

1.e4 d5 2.Qf3.strategy: Puts the queen on f3, where it eyes f7 and keeps e4 defended, but takes the best square from the king's knight. After 2.Qf3 dxe4 3.Qxe4 Nf6 the queen is hit and Black has the easier development.

1.e4 d5 2.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 but blocks the d-pawn, so White cannot build a pawn centre with d4. After 2.Bd3 dxe4 3.Bxe4 Nf6 the bishop is hit and Black gains a tempo.

1.e4 d5 2.Bb5+.strategy: Gives a check that gains nothing: 2.Bb5+ c6 attacks the bishop, and 3.exd5 cxb5 gives it up for a pawn. The bishop must retreat while e4 is still attacked, and Black has gained the useful …c6 for free.

1.e4 d5 2.a3.strategy: Ignores the attack on e4, so …dxe4 wins a clean pawn. The rook-pawn move does nothing for development or the centre.

1.e4 d5 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space and stops …b5, but leaves e4 attacked. After …dxe4 White is a pawn down with no development or central play to show for it.

1.e4 d5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 against g7, but leaves e4 hanging. After 2.b3 dxe4 3.Bb2 Nf6 the diagonal is closed and White has nothing concrete for the pawn.
1.e4 d5 2.b3.name: Scandinavian Defence

1.e4 d5 2.b4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Zilbermints Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.b4.strategy: Plays for Bb2 and a lead in development at the cost of the e4-pawn, and loosens the queenside. After 2.b4 dxe4 3.Bb2 Nf6 the long diagonal is shut and Black is a clean pawn up.

1.e4 d5 2.f4.name: Bird's Opening: Williams Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.f4.strategy: A pawn sacrifice that also opens the e1–h4 diagonal to the king. After 2.f4 dxe4 Black keeps the extra pawn, and White has little to show for it.

1.e4 d5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2 to support e4, but too slowly: …dxe4 wins the pawn first, and Black keeps it when the bishop arrives on g2.

1.e4 d5 2.g4.strategy: Ignores the attack on e4 and loosens the kingside, so …dxe4 wins a pawn. The pawn on g4 is weak and ties the queen to its defence against …Bxg4.

1.e4 d5 2.h3.strategy: Prepares g4 or stops …Bg4, but does nothing for e4. After …dxe4 White is a pawn down and Black develops freely.

1.e4 d5 2.h4.strategy: Advances the rook pawn with thoughts of h5, but leaves e4 en prise. After …dxe4 White is simply a pawn down, with a loosened kingside as well.

1.e4 d5 2.Na3.strategy: A rim knight that leaves e4 en prise: …dxe4 wins a pawn, and from a3 the knight eyes b5 and c4 without a target.

1.e4 d5 2.Qg4.strategy: Hangs the queen: 2.Qg4 Bxg4 captures it, because the c8-bishop sees g4 through the opened d7-square and nothing defends the queen.

1.e4 d5 2.Qh5.strategy: Aims at d5 along the fifth rank, but that pawn is defended. After 2.Qh5 dxe4 White is a pawn down, and …Nf6 then drives the queen back with tempo.

1.e4 d5 2.Ke2.strategy: Gives up castling and walks the king into the centre while e4 is attacked. After …dxe4 White is a pawn down, and the king on e2 blocks both the f1-bishop and the queen's diagonal.

1.e4 d5 2.Be2.strategy: Develops the bishop, but nothing guards e4. After …dxe4 White is a pawn down with no quick way to open lines in return.

1.e4 d5 2.Bc4.strategy: Hangs the bishop: the d5-pawn attacks both c4 and e4, so 2.Bc4 dxc4 wins a piece, and nothing recaptures on c4.

1.e4 d5 2.Ba6.strategy: Aims at b7, but the bishop is simply taken: 2.Ba6 bxa6 (or …Nxa6) wins a piece, and nothing recaptures on a6.

1.e4 d5 2.Nh3.strategy: Ignores e4 and puts the knight on the rim, where 2.Nh3 Bxh3 3.gxh3 wrecks the kingside pawns. Black can also simply play …dxe4 and win a pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.Ne2.strategy: Prepares Nbc3 or Ng3 against e4, but the knight blocks the queen and the f1-bishop. After 2.Ne2 dxe4 3.Nbc3 Black holds the extra pawn.

1.e4 d5.name: Scandinavian Defence
1.e4 d5.background: Arguably the oldest recorded opening: it appears in the Catalan poem Scachs d'amor (around 1475) and in Lucena's book of 1497. Bent Larsen's win over Karpov at Montreal 1979 spurred a rise in its popularity; in 1995 Anand played it against Kasparov in their PCA World Championship match in New York, its first appearance in a world championship match, and in 2014 Carlsen beat Caruana with it at the Olympiad in Tromsø.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn back at once with the queen, and accepts that White gains a tempo by attacking the queen with Nc3. In return Black gets a free game: easy development and a sound pawn structure, with no weakness to defend.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Delays the recapture so that the queen does not lose a tempo, and wins the pawn back with the knight later. White may try to keep the pawn, but usually just develops; the game turns more tactical, with Black aiming for quick development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nd7.strategy: Aims at ...Ngf6 and ...Nb6 to win back d5, but blocks both the c8-bishop and the queen's pressure on the pawn. White can hold it easily and stays a pawn up.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Na6.strategy: Heads for b4 to pressure d5 and c2, but the knight starts on the rim, and White holds the pawn with c4 or Nc3 and stays a pawn up.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Bd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's own pressure on d5 and does nothing to win the pawn back. White keeps it with c4 or Nc3, and the bishop on d7 is passive.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop but does nothing against d5, and White holds the pawn with c4 or Nc3 and stays a pawn up.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qd7.strategy: Attacks d5 along the file but blocks the c8-bishop. White defends with c4 or Nc3 and keeps the extra pawn while the queen has done nothing useful.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qd6.strategy: Attacks d5, but after 3.Nc3 White keeps the pawn, and the exposed queen can be hit with tempo, for instance by Nb5.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nh6.strategy: Aims for ...Nf5, but the knight on the rim does nothing for d5. White holds the pawn easily, and Black is a pawn down with a misplaced piece.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 a6.strategy: Wastes a move on a flank pawn and leaves d5 where it stands. White keeps the pawn with c4 or Nc3 and has lost nothing in development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 a5.strategy: Advances the a-pawn for no purpose: nothing is developed, d5 is not recaptured, and the move only weakens b5.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which would hit d5 along the long diagonal, but White holds the pawn easily and stays a pawn up with the better development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6.strategy: Offers a pawn for development: after 3.dxc6 Nxc6 Black's pieces come out quickly on open lines, but White stays a clean pawn up and can finish development in peace.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c5.strategy: Offers the c-pawn: after 3.dxc6 en passant Nxc6 the position is the same as in the 2...c6 gambit, a pawn down for some development. White can also simply keep the d5 pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e6.strategy: Offers the e-pawn: after 3.dxe6 Bxe6 Black has only the bishop out for it, and White stays a pawn up and develops freely.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e5.strategy: Grabs central space and opens the f8-bishop, but does not recapture on d5. After 3.Nc3 White holds the pawn with a developing move, and Nf3 then pressures the unsupported e5 pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 g6.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto, but the d5 pawn stays with White, who holds it easily and is simply a pawn up.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 h6.strategy: A waiting move on the rim: nothing is developed, d5 is not recaptured, and White holds the pawn with c4 or Nc3.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 h5.strategy: A wing advance that neither develops a piece nor recaptures. It weakens g5 and leaves White a clean extra pawn after c4 or Nc3.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nc6.strategy: Loses a piece: the d5 pawn attacks c6, so 3.dxc6 takes the knight, and ...bxc6 recovers only a pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Be6.strategy: Loses a piece: 3.dxe6 takes the bishop, and ...fxe6 recovers only a pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Bg4.strategy: Loses the bishop: nothing defends g4, and with the e-pawn gone from the diagonal the queen takes it at once with Qxg4.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Bh3.strategy: Loses the bishop for nothing: gxh3 or Nxh3 takes it, and no piece of Black's defends h3.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the queen's own pressure on d5, and 3.Bb5+ already checks the king on the open diagonal. The pawn stays with White.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 b5.strategy: Hangs a second pawn: 3.Bxb5+ wins it with check, and the d5 pawn is still White's.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 f6.strategy: Leaves the d5 pawn and takes the f6 square from the g8-knight. It weakens e6 and opens the e8-h5 diagonal for 3.Qh5+, damaging the king's cover for nothing.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 f5.strategy: Opens the e8-h5 diagonal: 3.Qh5+ is check at once and forces Black to weaken g6 or move the king, while the d5 pawn stays with White.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 g5.strategy: Loosens f6 and h6 and makes the g5 pawn a target for the c1-bishop once d4 opens its diagonal, while the d5 pawn stays with White.

1.e4 d5 2.d4 dxe4.strategy: Accepts the gambit and wins a pawn. White's compensation is quick development and open lines, so Black must take care to stay solid and avoid the traps that this opening is full of.

1.e4 d5 2.f3 g6.strategy: Develops by fianchetto, preparing the bishop for the long diagonal while the d5 pawn still presses e4. It is a modest answer to an awkward move: the better way to profit from f3 is to stake out the centre with a pawn at once, since White's king's knight loses f3 and the king's bishop has no good squares.

1.e4 d5 2.f4 dxe4.strategy: Takes the offered pawn. The pawn on e4 cramps White by controlling d3 and f3, and Black has nothing to answer for yet. White's compensation is only quicker development, so Black keeps the pawn while it is safe and gives it back at the right moment to finish developing.

1.e4 d5 2.g4 dxe4.strategy: Takes the e-pawn, and White has little to show for the loss. Grabbing the other pawn is not on: the bishop on c8 attacks g4 but the queen guards it, so taking loses the bishop. Black stays a pawn up and White's advanced g-pawn has weakened the kingside.

1.e4 d5 2.Nc3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn, which avoids losing the d5 pawn and opens the game. Black trades the d-pawn for White's e-pawn; White's knight now has to recapture or the position becomes a gambit.

1.e4 d5 2.Nf3 dxe4.strategy: Accepts the gambit, the usual and most critical reply: Black takes a pawn and attacks the knight, which must move. White is left with a lead in development to find, and Black's task is to hold the pawn without falling into the traps.
